articles.title: US ban on Canadian alcohol and dairy comes into effect as trade war drags on
articles.summary: It is the latest escalation in the Canada-US trade war after negotiations collapsed in late August, with no word on when talks may resume.
articles.body:
A US ban on several Canadian imports, including alcohol, dairy and motorcycles, has come into effect as a trade war between the two neighbours drags on.

The latest measure by the Trump administration is in response to Canada's implementation of tariffs on a range of US goods earlier this month following a breakdown in trade talks.

Canada is not expected to retaliate further, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying earlier this month that the impact the import bans will have on Canada's economy is "modest".

Trade talks remain on ice, with US trade representative Jamieson Greer telling CNBC recently that President Donald Trump is "comfortable" with his current relationship with Canada.

"They call us now and then and we have good conversations about potential deals. But there's no urgency on our side," Greer said of relations with Canada in an interview with the US network last week.

Tuesday's trade ban applies to nearly C$1bn ($710m; £530m) worth of Canadian liquor exported to the US, as well as whey products used in protein powder.

Motorcycle exports to the US will also be impacted, though Canada only sent about 5,000 motorcycles south of the border in 2025 that were worth about C$120m, according to national data by Statistics Canada, meaning the impact would be limited.

The import bans were first announced by Trump in a series of executive orders signed on 8 September. In them, Trump said the measures are in response to "continued discrimination" by Canada on US dairy, automotives and alcohol.

Speaking to reports on Monday, he accused Canada of "treating the United States very unfairly".

"They have been one of the worst countries in the entire world," Trump said.

What tariffs has Trump introduced and why?

Carney said earlier this month that the bans "are relatively modest measures" when compared to other trade actions the US has imposed on Canada.

He acknowledged, however, that the bans will hurt certain businesses and sectors that are directly targeted.

Derek Holt, an economist with Canadian bank Scotiabank, wrote in an analysis that "these actions are face-saving by the US administration, not substantive in nature and that's a positive".

About 93% of all Canadian liquor exports in 2025 were sold to the US. Spirits Canada, a group representing Canadian liquor producers, has said the consequences to the industry "could be significant".

Economists and businesses have also warned that the bans will add uncertainty to the future of Canada's trade relationship with the US, its largest trade partner.

In addition to these latest import bans, the US has imposed 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, including dairy, alcohol, steel and aluminium products, as well as 25% tariffs on Canadian-built cars.

Canada in return has placed retaliatory tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on more than 700 US products, as well as a 25% levy on certain steel and aluminium products. Most Canadian provinces have also stopped selling US liquor.

Tariffs - taxes paid on imported goods - are central to Trump's economic agenda, who argues that they raise government revenue and encourage consumers to buy American-made goods.

Economists, however, argue that they have raised prices of everyday goods for consumers and have disrupted the global economy.

articles.title: 8 US Marines hurt in previously unreported Iranian strikes; possible traumatic brain injuries: Report
articles.summary: Eight US Marines were injured in a previously undisclosed attack in the Strait of Hormuz on September 14, NBC News reported, citing three US officials.
articles.body: Eight US Marines were injured in a previously undisclosed attack in the Strait of Hormuz on September 14, NBC News reported, citing three US officials.The Marines were part of a battalion landing team when the missile hit the vessel, the officials said. Seven were enlisted personnel and one was an officer. None suffered serious injuries, but they experienced smoke inhalation and concussion-like symptoms, including headaches, with officials saying some may have sustained traumatic brain injuries.All eight returned to duty shortly after the attack, according to the officials.Marines were not aboard US Navy shipThe vessel struck in the attack was not a US Navy ship, according to the officials, who did not identify its type and referred to it only as a maritime vessel.The Pentagon did not publicly report the September 14 attack or the injuries at the time. The eight Marines were added to the Defense Casualty Analysis System nearly 10 days after the incident.One US official attributed the delay partly to injuries such as concussion symptoms that can take time to emerge, as well as the casualty database not being updated in real time.As of Wednesday, the Pentagon database had recorded 861 US service members as injured in the war with Iran, with the eight Marines included in that tally.Pentagon casualty figures under scrutinyThe disclosure comes as the Pentagon faces renewed scrutiny over how it reports US military casualties in the conflict.A Washington Post report said at least four US service members killed in the Middle East since the war began were not reflected in the official casualty count at the time. The Pentagon has also faced accusations of downplaying some injuries reported by wounded troops.The US military has disputed those allegations, saying casualty classifications such as “not seriously injured” and “combat casualty” have specific definitions that can be misunderstood.The newly reported Marine injuries add another previously undisclosed incident to the broader debate over how quickly US military casualties are recorded and publicly reported during the conflict.You use AI every day. articles.title: Viet Tan: Rights group accuses Vietnam of abducting Australian, Norwegian activists
articles.summary: Vietnam says the men entered the country illegally and accused them of planning terrorist activities.
articles.body:
A pro-democracy group has accused the Vietnamese government of abducting two of its members, an Australian and a Norwegian citizen, in Cambodia and taking them back across the border.

Vietnamese authorities confirmed that they had arrested Tran Hiep and Nguyen Duc Thuan, but say they had entered the country using forged documents and planned to carry out terrorist activities.

It said the men had admitted to being members of Viet Tan, which Vietnam sees as a terrorist organisation.

Viet Tan called their arrest a "blatant fabrication intended to conceal the fact that the Viet Tan members were abducted in Cambodia and forcibly taken to Vietnam".

The group, which has members in Vietnam and abroad, said the two men had been travelling in the southern border district of Kaoh Andaet in Cambodia when they went missing and had not been heard from since 18 September.

Tran's wife, Chloe Dang, told Australian media he had been meeting pro-democracy activists in Cambodia and had no intention of travelling to Vietnam.

He was meant to meet her in Bangkok to board a return flight to Australia but never turned up, she said.

"He always knew there was a risk doing human rights work, but we never thought that this would happen," she told the ABC.

According to a Vietnamese state media report published on Monday, Tran and Nguyen were detained with a third man at the border in Tay Ninh province on 18 September.

The trio "confessed to being members of the terrorist organisation 'Viet Tan,' [and] carrying forged documents to illegally enter Vietnam in order to carry out terrorist and sabotage activities," the report said.

They were charged on Monday with membership of a terrorist organisation while an investigation continued "to clarify the criminal acts of the suspects in order to handle them according to the law", it said.

"A state orchestrating the abduction of individuals abroad and forcibly taking them to its territory is a serious act of transnational repression," said Viet Tan. "It violates Cambodia's sovereignty and the fundamental principles of international law."

The Viet Tan statement did not mention the third man, who was named by authorities as Thai Cong Truong Son.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said consular support was being provided to Tran's family.

"That's what Australian governments do for our citizens. And we'll continue to engage directly with the family."

"Vietnam authorities' confirmation that they detained [these] activists... demonstrates yet again that Hanoi is arguably the most vicious and pernicious practitioner of transnational repression today in Southeast Asia," Phil Robertson, Director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates said in a statement.

"This latest act is an unacceptable outrage."

The Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Malaysia begins controversial repatriation of asylum seekers to Myanmar
articles.summary: Human rights groups say some 5,000 returnees could face violence, persecution and forced conscription.
articles.body:
The Malaysian government has started repatriating around 5,000 asylum seekers from Myanmar, under a controversial deal agreed with Myanmar's military ruler Min Aung Hlaing.

Three ships from the Myanmar navy are scheduled to leave Malaysia later today carrying the first 1,476 returnees.

Human rights groups have condemned the repatriation, saying the returnees face violence, persecution and forced conscription into the Myanmar army.

Malaysia has described the repatriation as voluntary, but has barred the UN refugee agency from seeing or screening the returnees, who have been kept in detention centres.

According to Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, these returnees will include Rohingyas: a persecuted Muslim minority who have sought sanctuary in Malaysia in large numbers after being driven out of Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens.

Anwar, whose popularity has fallen sharply this year, says he is responding to growing public hostility towards the large Rohingya population in Malaysia and has no choice but to negotiate with the Myanmar government over their return.

But the move signals a striking shift in attitude.

Anwar, a former political prisoner, has previously presented himself as a defender of human rights and freedom, and called for more to be done to help the Rohingyas. Under him, Malaysia has refused to recognise Min Aung Hlaing's regime, and has been one of the strongest voices in South East Asia pushing for a negotiated end to Myanmar's civil war.

Two things. First, increased economic strain on lower-income Malaysians since the Covid pandemic, which has stirred resentment of the Rohingyas.

Second, the febrile state of Malaysian politics since 2018, when a historic election unseated the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the ethnic Malay party which had monopolised power for more than 60 years, leading to a revolving door of unstable coalition governments.

For many years there was strong public sympathy among Malaysians for their fellow Muslims in Myanmar.

In August 2017, a brutal campaign by the Myanmar military drove three quarters of a million Rohingyas out of their homes in Rakhine State and into neighbouring Bangladesh. In the years since, dire conditions in Bangladeshi refugee camps have driven those with enough money to make the perilous sea journey to Malaysia in search of sanctuary and work.

While the Malaysian navy and coastguard have long tried to block Rohingya boats from landing in Malaysia, many gotten in via other routes, and for a long time were tolerated. More than 200,000 are now believed to live there, most eking out basic livings from manual labour.

Sentiment among Malaysians started to shift during the pandemic, which hit the country's economy hard. At a time of heightened public fear over the new coronavirus, accusations against Rohingya migrants spread on social media, with demands for their deportation.

In response, the then-government hardened its attitude, saying Malaysia could accept no more refugees and ordering raids on communities believed to be harbouring illegal immigrants.

In May, an online complaint claimed that Rohingyas had failed to dispose of animal waste properly after the Muslim Eid al Adha festival, igniting a viral social media campaign falsely accusing Rohingya leaders of demanding land and citizenship in Malaysia.

Shortly thereafter, an online petition on Change.org calling for Rohingyas to be kicked out of Malaysia received more than 400,000 signatures, before being taken down.

Given Anwar's one-time reputation as a champion of liberal values, he might have been expected to push back against this wave of hate and disinformation. He has said the Rohingyas should be treated humanely.

"We can arrest them, but do not beat, intimidate or humiliate them," he said in a recent podcast interview - although this is exactly what human rights groups have accused Malaysian officials of doing in immigration detention centres.

Nonetheless, Anwar insists that the Rohingya must be expelled.

"They have clearly become a burden," he said in the same interview. "A security burden, an economic burden and a source of hostility among the people."

Some of his former supporters have accused him of betraying his principles. The former head of the Malaysian Anti Corruption Commission, Latheefa Koya, says his decision is "disgraceful, amoral, and shames the nation in the eyes of the international community".

Anwar, though, is under great political pressure. Once described as a perpetual prime minister-in-waiting, he finally got the top job in 2022, but only by forming an uneasy coalition with his one-time adversaries UMNO. Since then he has seen his own popularity plunge and his party lose seats in recent local elections. He must call a general election by early 2028.

"He is in a corner, at his weakest point", says Tricia Yeoh, Director of the Asian Institute for Policy and Engagement at the University of Nottingham Malaysia.

"He has been forced to make concessions to his UMNO partners... There have been several corruption scandals, and his own party is divided. And after four years of telling voters this is what is required to maintain his fragile coalition, they are no longer willing to go along with that narrative."

Instead, Yeoh says, ethnic Malays, who make up more than half of the electorate, are responding to the well-trodden UMNO narrative that they need special support and protection from the state - the kind of racial politics which she says feeds fear and resentment of outsiders.

"It's the same narrative you hear in the rest of the world, about immigrants taking jobs, that we should not be spending our public funds on facilities for them."

However, it is not clear how any Rohingyas can be repatriated to Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens.

Rohingyas are not permitted to travel inside Myanmar, and are only allowed to live in Rakhine State, which borders Bangladesh. But nearly all of Rakhine State is now under the control of the insurgent Arakan Army, and subject to sustained bombardment by the Myanmar air force. On Monday, the day before the repatriation, the Arakan Army said two bombs killed 49 people at a market in the town of Kyauktaw.

The only place Rohingyas could conceivably be returned to is the state capital Sittwe - but it is besieged and isolated, and even there Rohingyas are confined to wretched camps which are critically short of food and medicine. Rights groups also fear that any men in the group could be forcibly conscripted into the army to fight in the civil war.

Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have explained how these formidable obstacles can be overcome, nor how their planned repatriation can be consistent with humanitarian principles.

"We all dream of being able to return home one day," said Nur Sadek, a Rohingya refugee rights advocate, "but we want to return because it is safe and because we choose to — not because we are forced to.

"For me, the most important thing is that Rohingya and other refugees affected by this decision are listened to and treated with dignity."

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack Jalud village in occupied West Bank, torch homes
articles.summary: A group of settlers attacked two homes belonging to the Al-Tubasi family in northern West Bank village.
articles.body:
Israeli settlers have attacked a Palestinian village in the northern West Bank, setting fire to homes, as Israeli forces raided several areas in the occupied territory.

In Jalud, south of Nablus in the northern West Bank, a group of settlers attacked two homes belonging to the Al-Tubasi family and set them ablaze, hours after the family returned under an Israeli court decision following nearly two months of forced displacement, the Anadolu news agency reported on Tuesday, citing local sources.

The fires caused extensive damage to the two homes, they said.

According to the sources, Israeli forces provided protection to the settlers and sent additional military reinforcements to the area.

The forces also compelled members of the Al-Tubasi family to evacuate their home again at gunpoint, the sources added.
